chunks: Where lost power goes and why it hurts. The question: What happens to any lost power? Why is this bad?
Power that a converter takes in but does not deliver does not vanish.
It turns into heat inside the transistors, the inductor, the copper traces (the board's wiring), and the controller.
That heat raises the temperature of the parts, which hurts reliability, performance, and battery life, and forces you to add heatsinks or fans.
Rub your hands together hard. The friction wastes some effort and your hands warm up. The harder you rub, the hotter they get. A converter's losses are the friction.
And just as your hands can only lose heat to the air so fast, a chip's temperature rises until enough heat escapes. If it cannot lose enough, it overheats.
The thermal-electrical analogy. P loss (a current source in watts) flows through theta JC and theta CA (resistors in °C/W) to ambient (a voltage source in °C).
The voltage at the top node is T J equals T A plus P( theta JC plus theta CA) . Anything that lowers either resistor, or lowers the current source, lowers T J .
Power loss: input power minus output power, turned into heat. Thermal resistance: how many degrees a part warms per watt of heat, in °C/W.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon inside the package. Thermal shutdown: the chip turns itself off to avoid damage.
Efficiency: see "Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement".
A regulator loses 1. 5 watts, and its package has a thermal resistance of 40 degrees Celsius/W. The temperature rise is 1. 5 times 40 equals 60 degrees Celsius.
In a 70 degrees Celsius enclosure, the silicon reaches 130 degrees Celsius, close to the 125 to 150 degrees Celsius limit that many chips have. That is the whole idea.
"Lost power becomes heat. The energy not delivered to the load is dissipated in FET and inductor resistance, switching transitions, magnetic cores and the controller's bias.

That raises junction temperature by loss times thermal resistance, which risks thermal shutdown and shortens component life, shifts parameters like on-resistance, wastes battery energy, and forces larger heatsinks and more cost.
So I compute the loss and check junction temperature at worst-case ambient."
